title: Prop-Firm Challenge Journal & Drawdown Guardian — Standard
description: Most prop-firm challenges are not lost on strategy. They are lost on one bad day — one session where the daily loss limit or the max drawdown gets touched and the account is gone. This is a record-keeping and self-review system built for exactly that problem. It is a journal and an organiser. You enter your firm's rules once, log your trades, and the workbook shows you — in dollars and in percent — how much room you have left before you break a rule. It tracks your daily loss limit, max drawdown (static or trailing) and consistency rule. If you searched for a prop firm consistency rule tracker, this is the records side of that job: your firm's best-day percentage cap is recorded in the firm-rules setup before your first trade, next to the daily loss limit and the drawdown floor, so the rule that can hold up a payout is written down while you can still act on it. What you get: - Workbook in Excel AND Google Sheets (same file, both formats), blank and ready to use - Firm-rules setup tab — you type in YOUR firm's rules: daily loss limit, max drawdown (static or trailing), profit target, minimum trading days. You set the numbers, so it works with any firm and any rule change - Trade log (500 rows) — instrument, setup, R-multiple, risk in dollars, screenshot link, and a mistake tag for every trade - Drawdown Guardian dashboard — shows your distance to your daily loss limit and your max drawdown limit in $ and %, with clear warning flags when 50% and 75% of a limit is used up - Analytics dashboard — win rate, profit factor, expectancy, average R, max drawdown, and an equity curve, broken down by setup, instrument, and session - Mistake tracker — your mistakes ranked by how much R they actually cost you, so you fix the expensive ones first - Weekly review page — a simple 10-minute weekly review routine, built into the workbook - Challenge-phase tracker — Phase 1, Phase 2, and a funded payout log - Worked example file — the same workbook filled in with 40 example trades, so you can see exactly how to use every tab - 24-page PDF checklist pack — pre-session checklist, tilt & risk checklist, challenge-day checklist, and a weekly-review worksheet you can print Who it is for: traders in a prop-firm evaluation, traders running a funded account, and traders about to buy a challenge who want their rules in front of them before the first trade. Please know: this is a journal and organiser only. It has no signals, no trade ideas, no predictions, and no financial advice. It does not connect to any broker or firm. It simply keeps your own numbers honest and visible. title: One Dinner, Every Eater: Picky-Eater Matrix & Exposure Tracker — Per-Child Food Matrix by Form & Texture, Exposure Ladder Log, One-Meal-One-Swap Week
description: You are not cooking three dinners because you lack recipes. You are cooking three dinners because what each child will actually eat — in which form, at which texture, on which day of a tired week — lives entirely in one exhausted adult's head. One Dinner, Every Eater is the data layer for that problem: a recording and planning system, not another meal planner. (If you want cooking and prep logistics, that's a different kit. This one is the per-child preference and exposure record that tells you what tonight's one dinner can be.) The Per-Child Matrix tracks every food the way children actually experience it: by form and texture . Because tomato is not tomato sauce — in the included EXAMPLE, Maya refuses raw tomato wedges and happily eats smooth tomato sauce on pasta, and those are two different rows with two different futures. Every food gets a status per child (Safe / Accepted / Will-Try / Refused), and running separately, in its own red column, the ALLERGY hard line: NEVER SERVE means never, in any form — and it is never confused with a dislike , because in a busy kitchen that confusion is the dangerous one. The Exposure Ladder Log counts for you. Feeding specialists commonly cite around 10–15 calm exposures before a food may be accepted — and this log auto-numbers every offer per child and per food (looked, touched, tasted and ate all count), with honest milestones: 'inside the learning range', never 'should be eating this by now'. In the EXAMPLE, Leo's broccoli ladder reaches exposure 12 — and you can watch it climb, one calm side-plate at a time. No cure is promised, here or anywhere in this kit. Some foods take longer; some are never accepted; the log tells the truth either way, which is what it's for. The Week Builder turns the record into dinner: one base meal per night, one small swap per child who needs it — a side plate, a different form, a sauce kept separate — never a second dinner. The shopping list underneath rolls up by formula from the week you planned. And the All-Eaters Table — the view the method courses and the $7.99 planners don't give you — puts every child on one page , food by food, with an at-table verdict per row (serve to everyone / accepted by all / needs a swap / ⛔ never serve), so the whole family's dinner gets decided from a single sheet. The Progress view closes the month in numbers, not verdicts: safe foods per child, foods in progress, tastes this month — the page to take to a pediatrician appointment if you ever want to, because 'here is what she eats and what we've offered' beats a vague worry. Pro ($37) adds the second-household system: a complete grandparent / other-household matrix workbook — because a food can honestly be Safe at Gran's and Refused at home, while the allergy hard lines travel word-for-word unchanged — plus the New Food Campaign Planner (PDF) : one food, one child, 15 exposures planned out in advance , with a form ladder for when the first form stalls. What you get — Standard ($27): Eater Matrix workbook (Excel + Google Sheets + pre-filled EXAMPLE, both formats) — 8 sheets, 388 live formulas: 3 per-child matrices by form & texture with the separated allergy hard-line column · All-Eaters Table with formula verdicts · Exposure Ladder Log with auto-count · Week Builder with formula shopping roll-up · Progress view Fridge Sheets (PDF, 4 pages) — weekly matrix snapshot, exposure ladder chart, week planner, allergy hard-lines page Parent Guide (PDF, 6 pages) — the no-shame method in plain words, the honest 10–15 exposure picture, running the matrix, allergy vs dislike, grandparents & other households Pro ($37) adds: the Second-Household Matrix workbook (Excel + Google Sheets + EXAMPLE) and the New Food Campaign Planner (PDF, 3 pages) . Who it is for: parents of selective eaters — especially with two or more children whose safe lists barely overlap — who want one planned dinner, a truthful record, and an end to holding it all in their head. Who it is not for: anyone looking for recipes, a nutrition programme, or a promise that a child will eat something. This kit records and plans; it does not treat, advise or cure — see Please know. description: If you have ever sat at the kitchen table, IEP in one hand and a nagging feeling in the other — the plan says twice a week, but is it actually happening twice a week? — this kit was made for you. The IEP Evidence & Meeting Kit turns that feeling into calm, dated records, in a file you own. Not an app. Not a phone tool your records disappear into. Not a binder of blank pages. A complete parent-side system: pay once ($34, or $44 for Pro), keep it forever, and walk into every meeting with numbers nobody can argue with — because every number carries its source. Start with the snapshot. Copy your child's services from the IEP services grid — service, minutes per session, sessions per week, location, provider. The workbook works out the mandated minutes per week by formula. Track what actually happened. Each week, for each service, enter the delivered minutes you can evidence — and choose where the entry came from: school log, provider email, your own observation, your child's report, or unconfirmed. That source column is the heart of the kit. Evidenced minutes count as recorded delivered. Child-report and unconfirmed minutes are shown in their own column — visible, respected, and never counted as delivered and never counted as missing . They are simply not evidence yet, and the kit treats them that way in every formula. Requesting the log is built in, not bolted on. When you don't have a log, the Records Request Tracker logs the ask (service, provider, date requested, date received, what arrived), and the kit includes a short, neutral fill-in template for requesting service logs / session records. Weeks still waiting print honestly as "unknown — log requested [date]" — never as assumed gaps. No-school weeks (holidays, closures, absences) are excluded from every total automatically. Every total follows one printed rule: mandated − recorded delivered = gap to discuss with the IEP team. That is the language the workbook uses, and the language you can use in the meeting: here is what the plan sets out, here is what the records show, can we talk through the difference? Then the two logs that make you the best-informed person in the room: a Communication & Incident Log (same-day, factual, printable as one clean record) and a Home Goal-Observation Log — what the goals look like at your dinner table, dated, in your own words. Finally, the Meeting Prep One-Pager builds itself : service figures and unknowns pull by formula from your tracker, ready to print with your top concerns and questions. Pro ($44) adds the long view: a Multi-Year workbook with a second full tracker and a summary that rolls the years together across annual reviews and school changes, plus a printable binder divider pack so the paper binder mirrors the file. Against the alternatives, plainly: a static binder organises paper but calculates nothing, and the premium ones cost about the same as this kit once shipping lands. A phone-based minutes tracker costs less — and keeps your child's record on a phone, in a tool you don't own. Advocacy courses cost $497–$1,200 and still leave you building the records yourself. This is the complete system — binder basics and the evidence engine and the home log and the meeting page — as ordinary files on your own computer. title: The CYA File — Teacher Defensive Documentation System: 5 Period-Based Logs, Meeting Pack & Counts Dashboard (Excel + Google Sheets Workbook
description: Description: "Document everything," they say. Nobody hands you the system. So it lives in a dozen Google Docs, a notebook you can't find, and your memory — which, three months later, in a meeting, is exactly as reliable as everyone else's. The CYA File is the system: five logs, one workbook, built for a real secondary timetable — up to 6 periods and 130–160 students, not one class of 25. The five logs (each with date, time, student initials and period dropdowns): Behaviour Incident Log — what happened, in observable facts, plus the action you took and the follow-up owed. Parent/Guardian Contact Log — who, method, a short factual summary, and the follow-up you promised. Both directions — including the contacts that went well. Accommodation Actually-Provided Log — the accommodation in the plan's own words, and the date it was actually given, lesson by lesson. This is the implementation proof. Admin-Request Log — the requests you were unsure about: who asked, what exactly, when, and your response, recorded at the time. Work Samples & Evidence Index — not the evidence itself; the index that finds it: what it is, where it is filed (district-approved places only), and when. The Meeting Pack is the page the whole file exists for. Type a student's initials, and live lookup formulas pull that student's counts and rows from all five logs onto one printable sheet. You walk into the parent meeting, the admin meeting, the review — with dates, not recollections. The Dashboard counts it all by formula: totals per log, incidents by period, accommodations provided counted by class period (rows marked Yes — so you can see provision period by period, not just as one total), counts by student, follow-ups still open. The Clipboard Quick-Log (printable) captures entries in the corridor in the moment; you transfer them to the workbook the same day. The Setup Guide includes the Privacy Rules page : initials instead of names, district-approved storage only, factual neutral language, same-day notes. What you get: CYA File workbook (Excel + Google Sheets + a pre-filled EXAMPLE) — 8 sheets: Setup (periods + rosters) · Counts Dashboard (40 live formulas, including accommodations provided by class period) · the 5 logs (40 rows each, dropdowns) · Meeting Pack (type initials → counts + rows from all five logs pulled by formula onto one printable page; 85 formulas) Clipboard Quick-Log (PDF, 6 pages) — cover + a daily capture sheet for each of the five logs Setup Guide (PDF, 4 pages) — setup, the daily habit, the Meeting Pack routine, the weekly ten minutes, and the Privacy Rules page Pro ($39) adds: the Factual/Neutral Language Phrase Bank (PDF, 4 pages) — say-this-not-that for incident notes, parent contact, and replies to admin requests, all original wording — the printable Binder Edition (PDF, 8 pages) — section dividers for all five logs plus monthly summary sheets — and the Admin Meeting Prep one-pager (PDF, 1 page) . Who it is for: general-education teachers — especially secondary teachers across 5–6 periods — who have been told to document everything and given nothing to document it in. Who it is not for: anyone wanting legal, contractual, or HR advice. This kit contains none, deliberately (see Please know). Please know: this is a documentation and organisation system only. It is not legal advice , does not interpret any law, policy, plan or contract, and does not replace your district's procedures or any professional guidance. The Accommodation Log records that an accommodation named in a student's existing plan was provided and when; it does not create, review or advise on plans. Record students by initials, and store this file and anything it indexes only in district-approved places. All worked examples use fictional initials and fictional situations, labelled as such.

title: Covered Summer: Camp & Break Coverage Planner 2027 — Coverage Grid, Camp Database, Registration Countdowns & Plan A-B-C Domino Tracker for Up to 3
description: Description: Summer is ten weeks. School is not in any of them. And for each child, every single week needs a named plan — a camp, a grandparent, a trip, cover — with its own registration window, deposit, balance and medical form. It is like a set of dominoes: if one falls, the whole summer falls apart. A waitlist that never clears strands a sibling's pickup, a leave week already booked, and a deposit already paid somewhere else. Parents who survive this well usually built the system themselves — one mother's own camp spreadsheet ran to 159 rows. Covered Summer is that spreadsheet, already built, and finished: the system a working parent would make if she had a free weekend and a formula habit. She does not. You are looking at it. title: Session Pack Ledger for Personal Trainers & Tutors — Sessions Remaining, Deferred Revenue, Expiry Flags & the Weekly Review (Low / Owes / Gone-Quiet)
description: Your booking app counts your clients. Nobody counts your packs — and packs are where the money quietly leaks. A client drifts away with six paid sessions unspent and never comes back. A pack expires and the conversation is so awkward you let it slide. A balance is "mostly paid" for four months. None of that shows up anywhere, because scheduling software rents you a diary, not a ledger. The Session Pack Ledger — Trainer Edition is the ledger, plus the operational layer the ledger alone never gives you. The Pack Ledger holds every client's pack: size, price paid, start date, expiry date , sessions used (counted from your log, not from memory), sessions remaining , and deferred revenue — remaining × per-session value, the money you are holding for work not yet delivered. Flags fire on their own: ⚠ LOW when a pack runs down, ⚠ PACK EXPIRED with the unspent count named. The Session Log runs on your rules: a Terms Toggle at the top decides whether a no-show burns a session, and every row, the ledger and the P&L obey it. Payment-vs-Balance puts pack value next to actually-paid for every client, with an ⚠ OWES flag — "mostly paid" becomes a number. And the hero: the Weekly Review . Every Monday it hands you three lists, pulled by formula, each with its action attached — LOW SESSIONS (≤2 left: send the renewal nudge before the last session, not after zero), OWES (send the reminder the same day; balances age badly), and GONE QUIET (no session in 21+ days: the win-back goes out while you are still their trainer). The Message Pack has the exact words for all five moments — renewal nudge, payment reminder, win-back, expiry warning, no-show reminder — warm, professional, with text versions and second touches for silence. The Pack Terms Printables give you the agreement one-pager (sessions, price, expiry, no-show and late-cancel blanks) and the sign-in sheet, so the terms the workbook enforces are the terms the client signed. The P&L Summary closes the loop: recognised revenue (sessions actually delivered) versus deferred, by month. Tutors: the same kit, built for how tutoring actually bills — per family. The Tutor Edition (included in this listing) is a Family Pack Ledger : the parent is the payer, every lesson is tagged with the student who attended, and both real pack models work — a shared pool siblings draw down together, and per-child packs under one bill , with per-child burn subtotals either way. Holiday freeze days extend the expiry date by formula. An early cancel earns a makeup credit — its own balance with its own expiry, never mixed into sessions remaining — and late cancels and no-shows obey your policy flag per family (burn / makeup / return) , never a hard-coded rule. The Parent Balance Statement prints one family's balance, per-child usage and sessions left, with a renewal line written by formula; the Tutor Weekly Review runs per family — LOW / OWES / GONE QUIET / MAKEUP EXPIRING SOON — and the Message Pack Tutor addresses every script to the parent: renewal nudge, statement cover note, makeup-credit notice, expiry warning, freeze confirmation. Tutoring platforms charge rent every month (TutorBird from $16.95/mo, Teachworks up to $187.99/mo) and their own reviewers complain that pack payments get applied to the wrong lessons; here the pack decrements per logged lesson, in a file you own. Pro ($37) adds the small-studio variant — the same ledger for 2–3 trainers, with a per-trainer roll-up of clients, sessions left and deferred revenue — and the Class-Pack sheet for prepaid group packs. The comparison writes itself: the platforms charge per client, raise the price as you cross client thresholds, and stack add-ons until a solo trainer is at ~$135 a month . Fifty clients costs $89.90/mo on PT Distinction's top tier — there, every month, forever. Here: $27 once. $0/mo, forever. The file does not get more expensive because you got busier; growth is not a pricing tier. title: Two Homes, One Plan: Co-Parenting Logistics Kit — Rotation Calendar With Overnights Maths, Shared-Cost Ledger, Handover Checklists & Communication
description: Description: The co-parenting apps are good. They are also built on one assumption: that both parents will join — and both keep paying, every year. The best-known ones run to hundreds of dollars per family, per year, forever. And if your co-parent never signs up — or signs up and stops opening it — the app keeps nothing, tracks nothing, and the organising lands back on you. It usually does. You are probably the parent reading this. Two Homes, One Plan is the version that works anyway. One parent, alone, pay once: $39 (or $49 for Pro). No subscription, no account, no app — and no requirement that your co-parent joins, installs or pays for anything, ever. You keep your copy, you keep your records, and the system runs entirely on your side. Yours forever. The Rotation Calendar does the schedule maths properly — the part parents quietly pay premiums for, because counting overnights by hand across a year is where mistakes breed. Set one start date and pick a pattern — week on / week off, 2-2-3, 2-2-5-5, or every-other-weekend — and the calendar generates all 365 nights, date by date. Life not matching the pattern? Type the real arrangement into the override column; your entry always wins. The Overnights Summary then counts it for you: overnights and percentage per parent, per month and for the full year, all by formula. (In the included EXAMPLE — a 2-2-3 year — it reads Parent A 183 nights, 50.1%; Parent B 182 nights, 49.9%. That is what "done correctly" looks like.) The Shared-Cost Ledger ends "split from memory, and later disputed." Log each shared cost the day it happens — what, who paid, the agreed split (50/50, 70/30, whatever yours is, per item). The sheet works out what each purchase does to the balance and keeps the running balance owed either way . No reconstruction, no screenshots of bank apps, no argument about a number nobody wrote down. The Communication & Incident Log is a clean record format: dated, chronological, factual — date, time, method, what was sent, what was agreed, what happened — written the same day, in plain words, and printable or exportable as one tidy record whenever you need it. The Handover Checklist (22 items, per child) is how the inhaler, the laptop and the cleats stop ending up at the wrong house. And the School & Medical Info Pack is one record of the facts — school, doctor, medication, allergies, contacts, authorised pickups — kept identically in both homes, so whoever has the children has the facts. Pro ($49) adds the year-level fairness tools: the Holiday-Year Planner — set who has each holiday once, and the next three years rotate automatically by formula, settled in advance instead of renegotiated every December — and the Settlement & Swaps sheet + printable Monthly Settlement Pack : set the month and the statement totals the ledger for you (paid by each parent, number of items, net owed, stated on an owed-to line ), ready to print and file with the month's receipts, plus a swap-request log that records every proposed date change with its agreed Yes or No. Against the file layer, plainly: the binders and printables under this keyword sell for $7.80–$25 and are mostly blank pages — no generated calendar, no overnights maths, no running balance. This is a system that computes. One $39 or $49 payment, once, against app bills of $168–$768 per family per year — and unlike the apps, it still works on the weeks your co-parent does nothing at all. What you get — Standard ($39): Two Homes, One Plan workbook (Excel + Google Sheets + a pre-filled EXAMPLE) — 7 sheets, 2,031 live formulas: Rotation Calendar (365 generated nights, 4 built-in patterns + custom overrides) · Overnights Summary (nights + % per parent, monthly and yearly) · Handover Checklist (22 items × 2 children) · Shared-Cost Ledger (running balance by formula) · Communication & Incident Log (dated, chronological, exportable) · School & Medical Info Pack for both houses Handover + Info Print Pack (PDF, 5 pages) — paper handover checklists per child + the two-house info sheet Setup Guide (PDF, 3 pages) — setup in about an hour, then minutes a week Pro ($49) adds: the Pro workbook (the same system plus the Holiday-Year Planner with 4-year automatic rotation and the Settlement & Swaps sheet that generates your monthly statement from the ledger) and the Monthly Settlement Pack (PDF, 2 pages) — the printable settlement statement with the owed-to line, and the swap-request log. Who it is for: separated or divorced co-parents — including high-conflict pairs, and especially the one parent doing 100% of the organising — who want correct schedule maths and undisputed cost records without betting the system on the other parent's participation. Who it is not for: anyone wanting legal advice, a custody tool, or a messaging app. This kit sends nothing and advises nothing — see Please know. Format: instant digital download. description: For solo pet groomers and small salons — this kit is sized for your business, not for a franchise. The Pet Services Business Kit runs the part of your business that happens between appointments . The Client & Pet Tracker holds every regular: owner, pet, breed, the coat and handling notes you currently keep in your head, each pet's groom interval, last groom — and the vaccination expiry date, with ⚠ EXPIRED and ⚠ DUE SOON flags calculated for you . The No-Show & Deposit Log records deposits taken, who showed, and what was kept under your policy, with a running kept total — the proof the policy pays for itself, and that you apply it evenly. Your Price List & Services is the one source every quote comes from, and a light Income Log & Snapshot shows the shape of the month without bookkeeping software. The Forms Pack matches the best-selling forms bundles at equal polish — client intake, service agreement/waiver, price-list menu page, appointment cards, a per-pet record card and a wall policies page — because your paperwork should look as professional as your grooms. The Reminder Message Pack is nine ready texts — rebook reminder, vaccination-expiry notice, no-show policy, deposit request, thank-you/review ask, plus peak-season, price-change, referral and long-interval messages — sent from your own phone, at $0 platform fee, with no cap . That is the anti-text-cap point: the messages that protect your diary are yours, unmetered. The Setup Guide sets the whole thing up in 30 minutes and keeps it running on a 10-minute weekly rhythm, including the policy-setting page where the deposit, cancel window and no-show rule get decided once, in writing, identically in the forms, the messages and the log. title: Medical Records Binder & Health Organizer — Health Records Tracker with Medication Refill Flags, Next-30-Days Appointment Pulls & Dashboard
description: For any adult organising their own health records — living with a chronic condition, parenting a medically complex child, facing a new diagnosis or surgery, or just tired of specialists who each hold one piece of your story and never see the rest. Your records live in six portals, a pharmacy app, a shoebox and your memory. None of those is where you are standing when someone asks. This organiser is the one place. The Health Records Tracker at the heart of this medical records binder is a living workbook, not a stack of pages. The Emergency Card & Profile holds the grab-and-go facts — conditions, allergies, blood type, emergency contacts, primary doctor, pharmacy — ready to print as a full-page card for the binder front and a wallet card for your pocket. The Medication Tracker carries every medication with its dose, prescriber, purpose written in your own words, start and stop dates — and the refill date, with a ⚠ REFILL OVERDUE / ⚠ REFILL DUE flag calculated by formula . You see the refill running out on the Dashboard at the start of the month, not at the pharmacy counter the night before a trip. The Appointment Log & Prep has the column no diary has: the questions to ask, written before the visit , while you still remember them — plus the outcome and next step, one line, the same day. Appointments in the next 30 days are pulled to the Health Dashboard automatically , alongside every refill needing attention and the counts of everything you have logged. The Lab & Test Results Log records each result exactly as printed — the value as printed, the range printed on the report — with space for your follow-up note. It deliberately never labels a result normal or abnormal: recording is the organiser's job; interpretation is your clinician's. Imaging and procedures, symptom and vitals notes as you record them , insurance and pharmacy card details, and your conditions and care team register complete the file. description: Description: Your prices were right once — on the day you set them, with that season's material prices. Then your supplier raised fragrance oil. Then the wax went up. Change ONE material price on the Materials sheet and every recipe reprices, every margin moves, and every SKU that has slipped below your target is flagged ⚠ BELOW TARGET — REPRICE BEFORE RESTOCK , with a live count of how many are flagged right now. That is the whole drift check: two minutes, before you spend money making more of something that stopped paying. When you act on a flag, the Reprice Decision Log remembers why — the date, the old price, the new price, and what drifted — so next season's you isn't guessing. The Setup Guide (10 pages) walks the whole system with worked numbers: the per-unit costing maths, labour and overhead without the self-deception, fees, the drift check step-by-step with the exact example figures, the three honest doors for a flagged SKU (raise it, redesign it openly, retire it), and notes for candles, soap & cosmetics, jewellery and ceramics. Standard formulas only, no macros: identical files for Excel and Google Sheets . Why not software? The inventory platforms that cost recipes charge $49/month and up — $588 a year, every year, with the best features gated behind higher tiers. This kit is a one-off $39/$49, holds 500 materials and 500 products with no caps and no gates, and leads with the one job they don't: telling you which of your products stopped earning. description: Description: This system starts from a fact every other planner ignores: the plan will break. A day will go missing. Then three. And a normal planner — organised by dates, with last Tuesday still sitting there blank — turns one missed day into a wall of guilt, so the planner gets closed, and then abandoned. Restart is the fall-behind-proof study system for teens 13–18, built for the day the plan breaks. Nothing in it is organised by date. Everything is organised by the state you're in. The One-Page Daily Sheet holds only today's 3 tasks — nothing else is allowed on the page, because everything else is what makes a planner feel like an accusation. Each task gets a tiny first step of two minutes or less. A task with a door is a decision. A task without one is just guilt with a deadline. The Weekly Sheet has the buffer built in — a planned catch-up slot, because the plan expects a missed day. Using the buffer is the plan working, not the plan failing. Learn to Study From Zero is the mini-guide for the student this system was made for: the smart kid who never learned how to study, because for years they didn't have to — until the work changed and the old trick quietly stopped working. In plain teen language (no lectures, no clinical anything): what studying actually is, active recall, spaced revisits, worked examples, the 25-minute session, notes that are useful later, the exam-season version, and a first week that asks for one small week that works — not a new personality by Monday. Part 2 is the Restart Moves Library: 60 concrete moves organised by state — Can't Start, Behind, Overwhelmed, Bored & Drifting, Exam Panic — so the help matches the actual problem in front of you. Across the whole system there are 105 counted moves, techniques and tools (the guide shows the arithmetic; nothing is rounded up). And because the other half of falling behind is the conversation at home, the Parent 10-Minute Sunday Check-In Script replaces the nightly homework interrogation with one short, same-time-every-week meeting: five questions in order, what never to say (and what to say instead), and how to run the reset together without it becoming a fight. Plus Task-Chunking Cards (PDF, 6 pages) — the three cuts that turn "write the essay" into pieces with a visible finish, with three big tasks cut for you — and Extra Reset Pages (PDF, 6 pages) — shaped resets for the three hardest moments: the week-3 wobble, the first days back after a holiday, and exam season. Who it is not for: anyone looking for a dated diary, a timetable app, or a system that works by making a student feel worse. title: First Car, Real Price — The Full True-Cost Workbook: True Savings Target, 4-Car True-Monthly-Cost Comparison, Insurance Quote Worksheet
description: A $4,500 car is not a $4,500 car. Before it has taken you anywhere, it also needs a year of insurance, fuel, a maintenance fund for the jobs every used car is hiding, and the state's title and registration fees. In this workbook's worked example, the honest total is $7,510 — the sticker was 60% of the story. Teens who save to the sticker buy a car they cannot afford to drive. This kit exists so you save to the real number. The full stack — every piece the $1–$5 savings-challenge cards leave out: Savings Target builds your TRUE target by formula: purchase price + first-year insurance + 3 months of fuel + maintenance starter fund + registration/fees. That total — not the sticker — is the headline number you save toward. Car Comparison prices up to 4 real cars (Pro: 6) on YOUR real commute — your miles, your local fuel price — and ranks them by true monthly cost . In the EXAMPLE, the cheapest car to buy ($3,800) is the most expensive car to run ($292.75/month), and the ranking proves it in one column. Insurance Quote Worksheet records the same driver and car quoted two ways — added to a parent's policy vs a policy of their own — with the monthly and yearly difference worked out for you (EXAMPLE gap: $160/month, $1,920/year). Record-keeping only: it never tells you which to choose. Fuel Calculator + Maintenance Sinking Fund turn guesses into monthly numbers, and roll a repair fund forward over 12 months so the first big job is an inconvenience, not a catastrophe. Afford-On-My-Hours Test asks the only affordability question that matters at this age: true monthly cost ÷ your hourly wage = hours of your life per week . The EXAMPLE car eats 5.22 hours a week against 12 available — verdict: FITS. If yours reads OVER, you find out at the kitchen table, not at the kerb. Savings Pace converts the true target into months: needed per month vs what you can honestly spare, the gap flagged when the wished-for pace doesn't work, and the reachable date that does. Plus the printable Inspection Checklist (bring a grown-up, check the VIN against the title, and the one line that saves purchases: an independent mechanic's check, booked by you) and the Buyer Guide — the true-cost story, private-sale vs dealer paperwork basics (information only), the first-year cost calendar, and the red flags that end a viewing. Pro adds the 6-car comparison workbook and the printable Savings Thermometer poster — colour a band per $250 toward the TRUE target. Why $19/$24 on a shelf of $1–$5 cards? Because those cards count savings toward a sticker price that was never the price. This is the only full true-cost stack on the shelf — target, comparison, insurance, fuel, maintenance, hours and pace, all computed — and the first credible full stack is the one that sets the standard. title: No More Chasing — Late & Missing Recovery System for Teachers (Grades 6–12): Slips + Regrade Queue, Overdue Flags + 3+ Missing Alerts + Parent
description: The late work isn't the problem. The chasing is. Across five periods and 180 students, here is how it actually goes: work lands on your desk with no name-day-context attached. Some of it gets marked, some of it sinks. A student reaches four, five missing pieces and nobody — including the student — can see the whole pile at once. The parent finds out at report time, which is exactly when it stops being recoverable. And Friday afternoon becomes you, a cold coffee, and a shoebox of slips, reconstructing a term from memory. No More Chasing replaces the shoebox with a workflow. Not a log — the shelf already has a $2.50 log, and a log only tells you what arrived. This is what happens NEXT, as one loop, held together by formulas: 1 · The slip. Every late piece arrives WITH a printed Late Submission Slip — student, period, assignment, due date, reason code — filed by the student, in the tray. No slip, no hand-in. The slip is their proof and your record, created at the only moment all the facts exist. 2 · The inbox. You log each slip once (the Friday routine takes 10 minutes total) and Days Late calculates itself, next to the reason code and the policy YOU set on the policy page — the same rule for every student, because the system applies it, not your mood at 4 PM. 3 · The regrade queue. Every ungraded late item pulls ITSELF into the Regrade Queue by formula, ages there by formula, and flags ⚠ OVERDUE the day it passes your regrade window (you set it — 5 school days is the standard). Mark it, tick one cell, and it leaves the queue by itself. 4 · The 3+ flag. The Missing Register counts missing work per student per period, and any student reaching 3+ missing is auto-flagged ⚠ — worst-first, every Friday, no head-counting across 200 students. One missing piece is an accident; three is a student going under, and now you see it the week it happens. 5 · The top-3 recovery list. Type the flagged student's name and period: their three highest-value missing items pull in by points , ranked. That's the 90-second recovery conversation — "these three, these dates" — instead of a hopeless list of nine. 6 · The parent update. The counts (missing now / late pieces in / awaiting regrade) are already calculated per student and select the right template for you: Template A (3+ missing, with the agreed recovery plan), Template B (the gentle nudge), Template C (good news — send those too). Polite, factual, two minutes, sent while recovery is still possible. The System Guide (6 pages) runs the whole thing: the Friday 10-minute routine step by step, the set-your-policy-once page, what to do at gradebook close, and a worked Friday read straight from the included EXAMPLE workbook, so you can watch the loop close on fictional students before trusting it with real ones. Pro ($27) adds the 6-period workbook variant (same system, pre-built for six periods, with its own EXAMPLE), the printable classroom poster of the late-work routine for above the tray, and the Amnesty-Week Planner — the term-end week, planned day by day, that lets a class dig out before the gradebook freezes. What you get (Standard, $19): Recovery Workbook (Excel + Google Sheets, blank + filled EXAMPLE) · Late Submission Slips (printable PDF, 6 per file) · System Guide with the routine, policy page and all three parent templates (PDF, 6 pages). Who it is for: middle and high school teachers (grades 6–12) teaching multiple periods — anyone whose late-work system is currently a pile, a memory, and a hope. Who it is not for: teachers who only need a simple arrival log (cheaper logs exist and are fine for that), and anyone whose school mandates a specific gradebook workflow that replaces this one. Format: instant digital download. Workbooks are .xlsx for Excel with identical Google Sheets versions (only Sheets-compatible formulas); slips, poster and guide are print-ready PDFs (US Letter). Please know: organisation and record-keeping only — not legal advice, and this kit does not set your grading policy; your school's late-work, grading and records policies outrank anything here. Keep student data minimal and private: the workbook is designed for initials or school ID numbers only, with no sensitive notes, and all students in the EXAMPLE workbook are fictional.

title: Travel Agent Kit — Travel Agent Business Kit with Client Proposal & Itinerary Templates, Commission Tracker Spreadsheet, Client Payments & Balances
description: Travel agent business kit — the system behind the proposal, not just the proposal. If you sell travel, you already know how to make a quote look beautiful; the $14 template shops have that covered. description: You run five to thirty subcontractors a year. title: Homestead Planner — Whole-Property Homestead Operating System: Seasonal Calendar, Garden Plan, Livestock Log with Check Flags, Preserving & Pantry
description: Homestead planner is a phrase that usually means a paper log book — pretty pages for the garden, the animals, the pantry and the money, in four separate places, none of which can add up a column. This Homestead Planner is the operating-system version: one workbook that runs the whole property . The Garden Plan keeps beds and crops light and honest: your sow date plus your own days-to-harvest estimate becomes an Expected Harvest date, calculated — no planting advice, your dates, your arithmetic done for you. The Livestock Log holds every animal group with its count, the feed you record, and health-check dates that become a NEXT CHECK date with ⚠ OVERDUE and due-soon flags — and it totals your production by unit, so the month's eggs and milk are numbers, not impressions. The Preserving & Pantry Inventory tracks every batch and shelf item with QTY LEFT calculated (in minus used) and low-stock and use-by flags from the dates you enter. The Equipment & Maintenance sheet turns last service + your interval into a NEXT DUE date, flagged before the season that needs the machine . And Budget & Sales closes the loop the log books never close: everything bought, everything sold, a monthly snapshot and a net by formula . A fully-filled EXAMPLE — a fictional 5-acre homestead in mid-season, 52 animals and hives, 83 units left in the pantry, $606 in sales against $458 in costs — proves every formula before you trust it with your own numbers. The printable Seasonal Wall-Planner Pack puts the year on the wall where the kettle is, and the Setup Guide sets the whole system up in 45 minutes and runs it on a ten-minute Monday round. This Planner deepens that garden layer into a whole-homestead OS — the garden sheet here is deliberately lighter, because the livestock, pantry, equipment and money sheets carry equal weight. description: Start with a website accessibility audit checklist — not with guesses, and not with promises nobody can keep. This binder is a complete WCAG audit template spreadsheet system: the ADA website compliance checklist for small business work, organised page by page and element by element; an accessibility remediation tracker that gives every failure a severity, an owner, a fix date and a re-test result; a website accessibility report template for clients you can actually send; and a plain, repeatable answer to how to audit a website for accessibility — keyboard pass, zoom pass, then images, contrast, forms, navigation and media, with everything written down. It is an organisational records tool: it organises the audit and the fixes. It is not legal advice, it is not a certification, and it does not guarantee that a site complies with any law or standard. The WCAG Audit Checklist carries 27 pre-filled checks organised by the four WCAG principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) and by element category, each with a Pass / Fail / N/A / Not tested dropdown and a pass-rate formula at the top. The per-element sheets do the detailed work: the Images & Alt Text Audit (one row per image — purpose, alt present, alt quality, and the exact replacement text), the Contrast Log (record the measured ratio and the minimum required; the Pass/Fail result is a formula , never a guess by eye), the Forms & Navigation Audit (labels, error wording, keyboard order, focus, menus), and the Media Audit (captions, transcripts, autoplay and pause controls). The Pages Inventory counts audited and in-progress pages by formula, and the Re-Audit Schedule computes each area's next-due date ( EDATE formula ) because accessibility decays with every new page, photo and plugin. Every failure lands in the Remediation Tracker : issue in plain words, page, WCAG reference, severity (Critical / High / Medium / Low) , owner, dates found, due and fixed, days-to-fix by formula , and the rule this binder never breaks — fixed is not closed; fixed and re-tested is closed , with the re-test result and date on the same row. Its summary (total, Critical, High, fixed & re-tested, % remediated) is pulled by formula, so the report you write from it cannot quietly inflate the progress. The Accessibility Audit Guide (PDF, 6 pages) teaches the whole method, including the traps: why an automated checker's "0 errors" is a starting point and not a conclusion, why a bolt-on widget repairs nothing underneath it, and why an accessibility statement must never claim more than the audit verified. The Audit Report & Statement Templates (PDF) give you the printable client-ready report (scope, method, results at a glance, findings by severity, what was fixed, what remains, limitations) and a draft accessibility statement whose known-issues list matches your report exactly. title: Fashion Tech Pack System — Clothing Tech Pack Template with Size Charts, BOM & Costing Sheets — Standard
description: Your fashion tech pack is the only thing standing between the garment in your head and the garment the factory actually sews. When it lives in scattered messages, a sketch and a spreadsheet that doesn't add up, the sample comes back wrong — and the re-make costs more than the pack ever would. This clothing tech pack template is the complete tech pack for manufacturing , in one workbook per style, with the maths done by formula. The Points of Measure sheet carries every measurement with its POM code, plain-English how-to-measure note, base-size spec and tolerance — and the graded sizes XS–XL calculate themselves from the grade increment you set. Change the base spec and the whole size run re-grades. The Bill of Materials lists every component — fabric, rib, cord, eyelets, labels, hangtag, bag, thread — with line costs and the materials total calculated for you . The Costing Sheet pulls that total in by formula, adds labour, overhead and freight, and gives you the unit cost, the wholesale margin, the retail margin, the markup — and the prices you'd need for the margins you want . Construction notes in sewing order, a Sample Tracker (proto / fit / PP / production, dated, with status), and a Revision Log so every change is versioned and provable complete the pack. A filled EXAMPLE — fictional Marlo Studio's MS-H01 unisex hoodie, 12 POMs graded, BOM totalled at $13.46, unit cost footed at $22.96 — shows the whole system working before you enter a single number of your own. The printable Tech Pack Template (PDF, 8 pages) is the paper twin for the factory packet: style page, front and back fashion flat sketch grid pages, POM pages, BOM page, construction page, and the costing/revision/sign-off page. The Tech Pack Guide (6 pages) walks through how to measure, how to grade, how to comment on samples so factories fix numbered problems instead of negotiating adjectives, and a full costing walkthrough. Pro ($49) adds the range tools: Full Grade Rules (every POM across every size for the pattern cutter), a Multi-Style Line Sheet (the whole range on one page — per-style unit costs, margins and line values by formula), a Factory QC Checklist (defect rates and AQL-style pass/fail calculated per checkpoint), and the Care & Label Spec sheet (fibre content, care wording and label placements in one factory-ready page). What you get: Tech Pack Workbook (Excel + Google Sheets + pre-filled EXAMPLE) — Style Header · Points of Measure with graded sizes by formula · Bill of Materials · Construction Notes · Costing Sheet with margins by formula · Sample Tracker · Revision Log Tech Pack Template (PDF, 8 pages) — printable cover/style, front + back flat-sketch grids, POM, BOM, construction, costing/sign-off Tech Pack Guide (PDF, 6 pages) — measuring, grading, factory communication, costing walkthrough Pro ($49) adds: Pro Extras workbook — Full Grade Rules + Multi-Style Line Sheet + Factory QC Checklist + Care & Label Spec (Excel + Google Sheets + EXAMPLE). Who it is for: indie labels, fashion designers and small brands producing with a factory or sample room. Who it is not for: anyone wanting a designer to create the pack for them — this is the system to build your own, style after style. Format: instant digital download. Workbooks as .xlsx for Excel with identical Google Sheets versions; PDFs print-ready (US Letter). Standard ($29) is the complete single-style system. Pro ($49) adds the grade rules, line sheet, QC checklist and label spec. Pay once, use for unlimited styles — no per-style fee, ever. Please know: measurements, grades, prices and margins are yours to set for your garment and your factory; always confirm a first sample against the physical garment before bulk production. Fibre-content and care-label wording must match your garment's actual composition and your market's labelling rules. All EXAMPLE brands, suppliers, prices and measurements are fictional.

description: You hired the agents. Nobody is managing them. Your content agent, your reply agent, your research agent — each one lives in its own chat thread, bills on its own invoice, and fails in its own silence. You cannot answer the three questions that decide whether the fleet is working: What does one approved output cost me? Which agent is quietly getting worse? And what actually happened the last time one of them invented something? This is the command system underneath the fleet — the same structure the done-for-you agent programmes run internally, as files you own. Not another agent. Not another tool. The management layer. WHO THIS IS FOR A small-business owner or operator already running two or more AI agents on real work — content, customer replies, research, listings, bookkeeping support, outreach — whose fleet has outgrown "I check in on them sometimes." If you have one chatbot you play with, this is more system than you need. If agents touch customers, money or your name, this is the paperwork that keeps them honest. Agent Roster & Roles Register — every agent as a staff record: name, job, model or tool, human owner, status, and a monthly spend cap . The sheet pulls each agent's real spend from the Cost Tracker and shows % of cap — an agent drifting toward its cap is visible before the invoice lands. Task Queue & Output Log — every job the fleet touched: who it was assigned to, the runbook it ran, whether a human reviewed it, and whether it ended Done, Failed or Redo. The done rate computes itself. Cost Tracker — every API charge, subscription and tool fee against its agent, by cost type. The totals feed the Roster and the Dashboard. Per-agent averages and error counts by formula — the agent whose quality is sliding shows up in its own numbers, not in a customer complaint. Prompt & Runbook Library Index — the fleet's institutional memory: every prompt and runbook, its version, its owner, its review date, and whether it is Current, Needs update or Retired. Escalation & Failure Log — every failure written down: what happened, severity, the SOP step that handled it, the prevention that landed in the runbook, and whether it is closed. Weekly Review Dashboard — the fleet in thirteen numbers, all by formula: agents, tasks, done rate, spend, cost per output , spend vs caps, QA average, open escalations — and the kill / keep board , where every agent gets a decision and a written reason, every week. Forty-four tasks, $318.20 of spend against $360 of caps, 32 QA checks, six escalations — including the listings agent that invented product specs twice, blew its cap, scored 2.83 on QA, and got retired on the board, with the reason written down. Every number reconciles; every decision on the Dashboard is one you can trace to a row. Learn the system on their month before you trust it with yours.
